title: Senior's toolkit: .NET's linear collections
summary: List, Stack, Queue, LinkedList and Span: what each costs, the Try methods that avoid crashes, and when to pick which.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: .NET's linear collections
steps.body: You will almost never write a dynamic array or a linked list at work: .NET has them. What matters is picking the right one, knowing what each call costs, and using the methods that do not throw on an empty collection.

toolkit.what: The default collection: a dynamic array. Fast at the end, slow at the front.
flags: O(n): every element shifts or is scanned
allocate once when you know the size, no regrowth

toolkit.what: Last in, first out: undo, bracket matching, depth-first search without recursion. All operations O(1).
flags: Pop and Peek throw `InvalidOperationException` when empty
TryPop(out var x) / TryPeek(out var x)
toolkit.example: if (!stack.TryPop(out var open) || open != '(') return false;

toolkit.what: First in, first out, as a ring buffer: breadth-first search, job queues, buffering. Enqueue and Dequeue are O(1).
flags: the slow imitation to replace: O(n) per call

toolkit.what: A doubly linked list. O(1) insert and remove when you already hold the node, but slow to walk (no index, poor cache locality). It earns its place in an LRU cache next to a dictionary of nodes.
flags: O(1) with the node; `Remove(value)` is an O(n) search
toolkit.example:
var node = lru.AddFirst(key);
index[key] = node;          // later: lru.Remove(node); lru.AddFirst(node);

toolkit.what: A view over part of an array or string, with no copy. Slicing a span is O(1); `Substring` and `ToArray` allocate.
flags: parse parts of a string without allocating substrings

toolkit.what: A span over a `List<T>`'s internal array: the fastest way to loop over or modify elements in place in a hot path (`System.Runtime.InteropServices`).
flags: while you hold the span: the list may move to a new array
change a struct element in place
toolkit.example: foreach (ref var p in CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(points)) p.X += dx;

steps.prompt: `List<T>` grows by doubling its internal array. What does this print?
steps.explain: The first Add allocates room for 4; the fifth Add doubles it to 8 and copies the 4 items. Copies happen rarely enough that Add is O(1) amortised. If you know the final size, pass it as the capacity and skip the copies.

steps.prompt: The bracket checker crashes in production on the input `")"` with this. What is the fix?
options: A closing bracket arrived with nothing open. Use `if (!stack.TryPop(out var open)) return false;` instead of `Pop()`
Wrap the whole method in `try`/`catch` and return true
Push a dummy item onto the stack before the loop
steps.explain: The top frame is the framework; your code is the first frame with your file name: line 9, the `Pop()`. An empty stack here is a valid input that means "unbalanced", so handle it as a result, not an exception.

items: The frontier of a breadth-first search
Print jobs processed in arrival order
Rows you read once and then index by position
An LRU cache that moves an entry to the front in O(1)

steps.prompt: Drain a work queue without ever throwing on empty.
steps.explain: `TryDequeue` returns false when the queue is empty, which ends the loop. `Push` and `TryPop` belong to `Stack<T>`.

steps.prompt: A job processor uses a `List<Job>` as its queue: `Add` to enqueue, `jobs[0]` then `RemoveAt(0)` to dequeue. With 200,000 jobs waiting it uses 100% CPU and barely makes progress. Why?
options: `RemoveAt(0)` shifts every remaining element: O(n) per job, O(n²) for the backlog. `Queue<Job>` dequeues in O(1)
The garbage collector runs after every `RemoveAt`
steps.explain: Indexing is O(1); removing from the front is what costs. `Queue<T>` is a ring buffer that just moves its head index.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Default to `List<T>`, and switch the moment you add or remove at the front (Queue) or only touch the top (Stack). Use the `Try` methods wherever empty is a normal case, and give a list its capacity when you know the size.
